\chapter{Seven Letters, and the Words You Already Knew}
\label{ch:ur-script-seven}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write seven Urdu letters from memory, read salam, kya, kan, nak, lal, kala, nila and lena off the page rather than from the romanization, and explain why Urdu leaves its short vowels unwritten.}

Eight words the book had only ever given by ear, read letter by letter from the right -- including kan and nak, the same three letters in different orders, which is the proof that the reader is decoding rather than recognising.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[alif]{\ur{ا} — one stroke, and a page that runs the other way}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-alef}



\begin{quote}
You have been reading Urdu words in this book for fifteen chapters and taking their shapes on trust. That stops here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — first, which way the page runs}
English marches \textbf{left to right}. Urdu marches \textbf{right to left}. Your pen starts at the \textbf{right edge} of a word and travels \textbf{towards the left}, so the letter you meet \textbf{first} is the \textbf{rightmost} one.

There is a second direction, and it belongs to Urdu in a way it does not belong to Arabic. Urdu is written in a style called \textbf{Nastaliq}, and Nastaliq does not sit flat on the line. A word \textbf{cascades downward as it moves left}, each letter hanging a little below the one before it, so a word reads like a short diagonal staircase running down to the left.

That is why Urdu looks different from Arabic even where the letters are the same. It is not decoration and it is not optional: it is how Urdu is set.

\subsection*{Script — the letter itself}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ا}
\end{quote}

\textbf{One tall downstroke.} Draw it from the top down and lift. Nothing else.

Its name is \textbf{alif}, and one thing about it matters more than its shape: \textbf{alif does not join to the letter that follows it.} Hold that; the next few lessons will make it pay.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ا} — one stroke, top to bottom
  \item \emph{Point to:} at the right edge of an Urdu word, where your pen would begin
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many strokes in alif? (\textbf{One}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lām]{\ur{ل} — alif, and then a bowl under the line}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-lam}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ا}. One stroke, top to bottom.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ل}
\end{quote}

Start exactly as you started alif — a tall upright coming down — and then, without lifting, \textbf{carry on below the baseline} into a leftward bowl and back up.

One movement, no pen lift. The bowl going \textbf{below the line} is the part to get right; it is what tells lām apart from alif at a glance.

Its name is \textbf{lām} and it says \textbf{l}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ا}, then \ur{ل} — the same descent, then the bowl below the line
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{l}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Do you lift the pen between the upright and the bowl? (\textbf{No}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sīn]{\ur{س} — three teeth, then a bowl, without lifting}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-sin}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ل}. Upright, then the bowl below the line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{س}
\end{quote}

Three small \textbf{teeth} close together — short upward points in a row — and then the line flows straight on into a \textbf{bowl} below the baseline.

Remember which way you are working: the first tooth you draw is the \textbf{rightmost} one.

\textbf{No lift anywhere.} Teeth and bowl are one continuous movement, and letting the pen stop between them is the commonest way a beginner's sīn comes out looking like two letters.

Its name is \textbf{sīn} and it says \textbf{s}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{س} — three teeth from the right, flowing into the bowl, one movement
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{s}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which tooth comes first? (The \textbf{rightmost}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mīm]{\ur{م} — a round head, and a tail under the line}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-mim}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{س}. Three teeth, then the bowl, no lift.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{م}
\end{quote}

A small \textbf{round head} sitting on the line, and from it a \textbf{tail} running straight down \textbf{below} the baseline.

Keep the head small and closed. Plenty of letters dip below the line — you have already written one in lām — but mīm's drop is a \textbf{straight tail} hanging off a round head, and that combination is what makes it easy to spot standing alone. Joined into the middle of a word the tail is trimmed away and the head survives.

One movement, no lift.

Its name is \textbf{mīm} and it says \textbf{m}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{م} — the round head, then the tail below the line
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{m}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the head open or closed? (\textbf{Closed}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[salām]{Letters that hold hands, and the one that will not}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-joining}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{س}, then \ur{م}. Four letters are now yours.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the running, falling line}
Urdu letters \textbf{join}. They run into one another along a single connected line, and because this is Nastaliq that line is also \textbf{falling} — each joined letter sits a little lower and further left than the one before it.

Because they join, most letters \textbf{change shape} by position. A letter opening a joined run, one buried in the middle, one closing it, and one standing alone can all look different. They are the same letter.

That sounds like four times the work and it is not, because the change is almost always \textbf{the same trimming}: the part that identifies the letter stays, and the finishing flourish is cut short so the next letter can start. You saw it already in mīm, where joining costs the tail and keeps the head.

\subsection*{Script — and the letter that refuses}
Now the rule that saves the most confusion.

\textbf{Some letters take the hand of the letter on their right and offer nothing to the left.} The run stops dead after them, and the next letter begins as though starting a fresh word.

\textbf{alif is one of these.} So a gap in the middle of an Urdu word is usually not a word break at all — it is a non-joining letter doing exactly what it always does. Without that fact a page of Urdu looks like it has been spaced at random.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four letters, and they spell the word this book opened with:

\begin{quote}
\ur{سلام}
\end{quote}

From the right: \textbf{\ur{س}} \emph{s}, \textbf{\ur{ل}} \emph{l}, \textbf{\ur{ا}} \emph{ā}, \textbf{\ur{م}} \emph{m}. Say it: \textbf{salām}.

Two things to see. The short vowel between s and l is \textbf{not written} — Urdu prints the long vowels and leaves the short ones to the reader. And the break before the final \ur{م} is alif refusing to join, exactly as promised.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{سلام} — name each letter from the right, then say the word
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{سلام} — let the line fall as it goes, and let it break after alif
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{salām}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does mīm lose when it joins? (Its \textbf{tail}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāf]{\ur{ک} — a bowl with a slash laid over it}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-kaf}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{سلام}. Four letters, one break.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ک}
\end{quote}

Two movements, and exactly \textbf{one} lift between them.

1. a \textbf{stem} down, flowing right to left through a \textbf{flatter bowl} and finishing with a pronounced \textbf{hook} — all without lifting 2. lift once, then a \textbf{long slash} drawn down from the upper right towards the stem

The slash is not a dot and not decoration; it is part of the letter, and leaving it off writes nothing at all.

Its name is \textbf{kāf} and it says \textbf{k}.

Worth knowing: \textbf{this is the Urdu kāf.} Arabic writes the same sound with a different shape, and if you have seen Arabic you will notice the difference immediately. Urdu keeps the Perso-Arabic alphabet and does not keep every Arabic shape.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ک} — stem, bowl and hook in one movement, then lift and lay the slash across
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{k}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the slash optional? (\textbf{No} — without it the letter is not written.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nūn]{\ur{ن} — a deep bowl, and one dot}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-nun}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ک}. Bowl and hook, lift, slash.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ن}
\end{quote}

A \textbf{bowl} swept from right to left, dropping well \textbf{below the baseline} and rising again — then one lift, and a single \textbf{dot} placed near the baseline, inside the curve.

Two parts, one lift. The bowl is deeper and rounder than the flatter one you drew in kāf, and the dot sits low rather than floating above.

Its name is \textbf{nūn} and it says \textbf{n}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ن} — the deep bowl, then lift and place the dot low inside it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{n}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which bowl is deeper, nūn's or kāf's? (\textbf{nūn's}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye]{\ur{ی} — one S-curve, no dots}

\label{lesson:UR-W16-ye}



\begin{quote}
Write \ur{ن}. Deep bowl, lift, low dot.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\ur{ی}
\end{quote}

Start at the \textbf{upper right} and descend through an \textbf{S-shaped curve}, then carry on left around a bowl that drops \textbf{below the baseline}, and finish at its rising tip.

\textbf{One movement. No lift, and no dots at all.} Standing alone, ye is one of the few letters in this chapter with nothing added to it — no dot, no slash — and that emptiness is how you recognise it.

Its name is \textbf{ye}, and it does \textbf{three} jobs: the consonant \textbf{y}, the long vowel \textbf{ī}, and a second long vowel \textbf{e}. Which one it is comes from the word, not from the shape — there is nothing on the page to tell them apart.

You will meet all three in this chapter. \textbf{\ur{کیا}} \emph{kyā} uses the consonant, \textbf{\ur{نیلا}} \emph{nīlā} uses the long \emph{ī}, and \textbf{\ur{لینا}} \emph{lenā} uses the \emph{e}. Three words, one letter, three values, and only having heard them tells you which.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{ی} — the S-curve down, round the bowl, and up at the tip
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{y}, then \textbf{ī}, then \textbf{e} — one letter, three jobs
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Can the shape alone tell you which of its three values it carries? (\textbf{No} — the word tells you.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — eight words you already knew, now read}

\label{lesson:UR-C16-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write your seven letters in a row, right to left, naming each as you go, and let the line fall as it travels.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the words come back}
\textbf{Nothing new is taught here.} Every word below was already given to you to say, and every letter in it is one you can now write.

Read each from the right, naming its letters before you say it:

\begin{quote}
\ur{سلام}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کیا}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کان}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{ناک}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{لال}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{کالا}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{نیلا}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\ur{لینا}
\end{quote}

\emph{salām} — \emph{kyā} — \emph{kān} — \emph{nāk} — \emph{lāl} — \emph{kālā} — \emph{nīlā} — \emph{lenā}.

Eight words from seven letters. Two of them are worth a second look: \textbf{\ur{کان}} \emph{kān} \textquotedblleft{}ear\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ur{ناک}} \emph{nāk} \textquotedblleft{}nose\textquotedblright{} use the \textbf{same three letters} in different orders, which is the clearest possible proof that you are reading rather than recognising a picture.

\begin{culture}
Count the letters in \textbf{\ur{کیا}} and count the sounds in \emph{kyā}.

\textbf{Urdu writes its long vowels and leaves the short ones off the page.} The reader supplies them. That is why \emph{salām} has a vowel between the s and the l that nothing on the page records.

This has a consequence worth accepting now rather than discovering later: \textbf{you cannot reliably sound out an Urdu word you have never heard.} Reading and listening have to grow together here, more tightly than in a language that spells every vowel — which is exactly why this book spent fifteen chapters putting these words in your ear before handing you the page.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Seven letters, and three ideas that outlast them:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the page runs right to left}, and in Nastaliq the word also \textbf{falls} as it goes, each letter hanging below the last
  \item \textbf{letters join}, changing shape by position — but the change is a \textbf{trimming}, and \textbf{alif refuses to join leftward}, which is what puts gaps inside a word
  \item \textbf{what is added matters}: nūn's dot, kāf's slash, and ye's bare curve are the identification, not the decoration
\end{itemize}

Seven of Urdu's letters. The rest are mostly more of what you just did.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کان} and \ur{ناک} — same three letters, and say which is which
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{سلام} — and let it break after alif
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کالا} \ur{نیلا} \ur{لال} — name the letters of each before saying it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of your seven letters refuses to join to the left? (\textbf{\ur{ا}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
